content: Dental fear, also known as dental anxiety or dental phobia, is the fear of dentistry and receiving dental care. In its pathological form, it is referred to as a specific phobia and may be called dental phobia, odontophobia, dentophobia, or dentist phobia. Studies estimate that up to 75% of adults in the United States experience some level of dental fear, ranging from mild to severe. A smaller percentage of individuals suffer from dental phobia, where the fear is so intense that they avoid dental care entirely, even when it is necessary. Many people with dental fear only seek treatment during emergencies, such as when they experience a toothache or develop a dental abscess. This avoidance often leads to a cycle of avoidance, where fear prevents regular care, resulting in emergencies that require invasive treatments, which in turn reinforce the fear. Women are more likely to report dental fear than men, and younger individuals tend to report higher levels of fear compared to older adults. People are generally more fearful of invasive procedures, such as oral surgery, than they are of less invasive treatments like professional dental cleanings or prophylaxis. The causes of dental fear often stem from traumatic, difficult, or painful dental experiences in the past. Fear can also develop indirectly, such as through hearing about others' negative experiences or through exposure to negative portrayals of dentistry. Treatment for dental fear typically involves a combination of behavioral and pharmacological techniques. Specialized dental fear clinics, such as those at the University of Washington in Seattle and Göteborg University in Sweden, employ both psychologists and dentists to help patients manage and reduce their fear. These clinics aim to equip individuals with the skills necessary to receive regular dental care with minimal fear or anxiety. Outside of these specialized clinics, many dental providers also use behavioral and cognitive strategies to help patients manage their fear. Behavioral treatments include teaching relaxation techniques, such as diaphragmatic breathing and progressive muscle relaxation, as well as cognitive techniques like cognitive restructuring and guided imagery. These methods have been shown to significantly reduce dental fear. One specific behavioral approach is systematic desensitization, also known as graduated exposure therapy. For example, a patient fearful of dental injections may first learn relaxation skills and then gradually be exposed to the feared object (e.g., the needle or syringe) while practicing these relaxation techniques. Over time, the patient progresses to receiving a dental injection with little to no fear. This method has proven effective in treating fear of dental injections. Pharmacological techniques to manage dental fear range from mild sedation to general anesthesia. Dentists often combine these methods with behavioral techniques. One commonly used medication is nitrous oxide, or laughing gas, which is inhaled through a mask and induces relaxation and dissociation. Oral sedatives, such as benzodiazepines like alprazolam (Xanax), diazepam (Valium), or triazolam (Halcion), may also be prescribed. These medications help patients feel calmer and sometimes drowsy during treatment, but they remain conscious and able to communicate with the dental staff. Intravenous (IV) sedation involves administering benzodiazepines directly into a patient’s arm or hand. This is often referred to as conscious sedation, as patients remain awake and breathe on their own while their vital signs are monitored. In contrast, general anesthesia (GA) involves deeper sedation, where patients are not conscious. For individuals with dental fear, finding a dentist who is willing to work with fearful patients can be facilitated through recommendations from family, friends, dental insurance companies, or medical professionals. It is often helpful for patients to schedule an initial appointment with a new dentist to discuss their past experiences, concerns, and fears without undergoing any treatment during that visit. Additionally, some individuals find online dental fear support resources to be beneficial.
